The Imperial Food Products Case

On September 3, 1991, a fire broke out at Imperial Food Products chicken processing plant in Hamlet, North Carolina. 25 workers were killed, 55 were injured. The fire doors had been locked to prevent employee theft — a decision that proved fatal. This case is used in every course to illustrate the critical importance of means of egress regulations.

Fire Tetrahedron & Flash Point

Fire Tetrahedron

The modern understanding of fire replaces the old "fire triangle" with a tetrahedron — four components, all required simultaneously:

Fuel
The combustible material — wood, paper, flammable liquids, gases, metals
Heat / Ignition Source
Energy to initiate combustion — open flame, sparks, hot surfaces, static electricity
Oxygen
Oxidizer (usually air with ~21% O₂). Fire requires minimum ~16% O₂ to sustain combustion.
Chemical Chain Reaction
The self-sustaining exothermic chain reaction — the 4th element added beyond the fire triangle.

To extinguish fire: remove any ONE of the four elements.

Flash Point & Fire Point

TermDefinitionSignificance
Flash PointLowest temperature at which a liquid produces sufficient vapor to ignite momentarily when exposed to an ignition source (but does not sustain combustion)Used to classify flammability hazard
Fire PointTemperature slightly above flash point at which vapors continue to burn after ignition source is removedSlightly higher than flash point

Liquid Classification by Flash Point

Flammable Liquid
Flash point < 100°F (37.8°C). Examples: gasoline (−45°F), acetone (−4°F), ethanol (55°F). HIGH hazard — can ignite at room temperature.
Combustible Liquid
Flash point ≥ 100°F (37.8°C). Examples: diesel (100–130°F), kerosene (100–165°F). Lower hazard — requires heating before vapor generation.

Flammability Limits (LFL/UFL)

LFL (Lower Flammable Limit) = LEL
The minimum concentration of fuel vapor in air that can ignite. Below LFL = too lean (insufficient fuel to burn). Example: methane LFL = 5% by volume.
UFL (Upper Flammable Limit) = UEL
The maximum concentration of fuel vapor in air that can ignite. Above UFL = too rich (insufficient oxygen). Example: methane UFL = 15% by volume.

The flammable range (between LFL and UFL) is where fire/explosion can occur. The wider the range, the more hazardous the substance.

Fire Classes

Fire Classification System (Mnemonic Aids)

ClassType of FireExamplesMemory Aid
AOrdinary combustiblesWood, paper, cloth, rubber, plastics"Ash" — leaves ash when burned
BFlammable/combustible liquids & gasesGasoline, oil, grease, paint, propane"Barrel" — oil barrels/fuel containers
CEnergized electrical equipmentElectrical panels, motors, computers"Current" — electrical current
DCombustible metalsMagnesium, sodium, potassium, titanium"Dynamite" — explosive potential of reactive metals
KCooking oils & fats (high-temp)Vegetable oils, animal fats in deep fryers"Kitchen" — restaurant/kitchen fires

⚠️ Important: NEVER use water on a Class B fire (fuel spreads and water vaporizes explosively creating steam that spreads burning liquid). NEVER use water on a Class C fire (electrical shock hazard). NEVER use water on a Class K fire (saponification — high-temperature oils can cause violent steam explosion with water).

Fire Extinguishers

PASS System — How to Use a Fire Extinguisher

P — Pull
Pull the safety pin from the handle
A — Aim
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire (not at the flames)
S — Squeeze
Squeeze the lever to discharge agent
S — Sweep
Sweep side-to-side while moving forward

Types of Fire Extinguishers

TypeExtinguishing AgentClassesMechanismID Color
WaterWaterA onlyCooling — removes heat from fire tetrahedronRed band
CO₂Carbon dioxideB, CSmothering (displaces O₂) + cooling. No residue — safe for electronics.Black band
Dry Chemical (ABC)Monoammonium phosphate powderA, B, CInterrupts chemical chain reaction; most versatile typeBlue band
Dry Chemical (BC)Sodium/potassium bicarbonateB, C onlyInterrupts chain reaction; does NOT work on Class ABlue band
Foam (AFFF)Aqueous film-forming foamA, BSmothers liquid fires; prevents re-ignition by forming vapor-suppressing filmCream band
Class DDry powder (specialized)D onlySpecialized for each combustible metal — do NOT use standard extinguishersBlue
Class KWet chemical (K₂C₂O₄)K onlySaponification reaction with cooking oil; cools and seals oil surfaceYellow band

Three Methods of Fire Extinguishment

Cooling (Remove Heat)
Water is the primary cooling agent. Absorbs heat energy, lowering temperature below ignition point.
Smothering (Remove Oxygen)
CO₂, foam, and dry powder blanket the fire, cutting off oxygen supply.
Starvation (Remove Fuel)
Remove or isolate the fuel source — close a gas valve, move combustible materials away from fire.

Means of Egress & Fire Protection Systems

Means of Egress (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.37)

Every building must provide adequate means of egress — unobstructed travel from anywhere in the building to a safe area outside. Three components:

  • Exit Access — the portion of the means of egress within the occupied area leading to an exit
  • Exit — the protected path of travel to the exit discharge (fire doors, stairwells, fire-rated corridors)
  • Exit Discharge — the path from the exit to a public way (open space outside)

Key Egress Requirements

  • Exits must be clearly marked with illuminated signs
  • Exits must remain unobstructed and unlocked during working hours (the Imperial Food Products lesson)
  • Minimum two exits required from any occupied area
  • Fire doors must be self-closing and not wedged/propped open
  • Exit routes must be wide enough for expected occupancy

Fire Protection Systems

Smoke Alarms
Test monthly; change batteries annually; replace entire unit every 10 years. Provides early warning for evacuation.
Sprinkler Systems
Automatic fire suppression — most effective. Each sprinkler activates individually at ~165°F. NOT like movies where all activate simultaneously.
Standpipe Systems
Piping system in multi-story buildings providing water to hose connections on each floor for firefighter use.
Fire Pumps
Boost water pressure in sprinkler/standpipe systems. Electric or diesel driven for backup during power outages.

Quick Review

What are the 4 elements of the fire tetrahedron?
Fuel, Heat (ignition), Oxygen, Chemical Chain Reaction. Remove any one to extinguish the fire.
What is the flash point cutoff for flammable vs combustible?
Flammable: flash point < 100°F (37.8°C). Combustible: flash point ≥ 100°F.
What are LFL and UFL?
LFL = minimum % fuel vapor for ignition (too lean below). UFL = maximum % for ignition (too rich above). Fire can only occur between them.
What class of fire does each letter represent? (A/B/C/D/K)
A=Ash/ordinary combustibles, B=Barrel/liquids, C=Current/electrical, D=Dynamite/metals, K=Kitchen/cooking oils
What does PASS stand for?
Pull pin, Aim at base, Squeeze lever, Sweep side-to-side
Why is CO₂ good for electrical fires?
CO₂ is non-conductive (no shock hazard), smothers by displacing oxygen, leaves no residue that damages equipment.
What are the 3 methods of fire extinguishment?
Cooling (remove heat) — water; Smothering (remove oxygen) — CO₂/foam/powder; Starvation (remove fuel) — close valve/move materials
What was the key lesson from Imperial Food Products (1991)?
Never lock fire exits during working hours. 25 workers died because locked exits prevented escape. Means of egress must remain unobstructed and unlocked.
